items.summary: BEIR contains 18 English zero-shot evaluation datasets drawn from 9 heterogeneous retrieval tasks.
items.notes: 'In total, we include 18 English zero-shot evaluation datasets from 9 heterogeneous retrieval tasks.'

items.summary: Counting MS MARCO there are 19 datasets; only 8 of the 19 have training data.
items.notes: 'Only 8 out of 19 datasets (including MS MARCO) have training data denoting the practical importance for zero-shot retrieval benchmarking.'

items.summary: The nine tasks are fact checking, citation prediction, duplicate question retrieval, argument retrieval, news retrieval, question answering, tweet retrieval, bio-medical IR and entity retrieval.
Datasets vary in size (3.6k to 15M documents), average query length (3 to 192 words) and average document length (11 to 635 words).
items.notes: 'datasets of various sizes (3.6k - 15M documents), and datasets with different query lengths (average query length between 3 and 192 words) and document lengths (average document length between 11 and 635 words)'

items.summary: Per-dataset statistics from the README table: test queries, corpus size, relevant documents per query.
items.notes: Agrees with paper Table 1 (e.g. TREC-COVID 171,332 docs, BioASQ 14,914,602, NFCorpus 3,633 at lines 236-245).

items.summary: Most datasets have binary relevance judgements; some have few relevant documents per query (<2) while TREC-COVID can have up to 500. All datasets except ArguAna have short queries (a single sentence or 2-3 keywords).
items.notes: 'All datasets except ArguAna [67] have short queries (either a single sentence or 2-3 keywords).'

items.summary: BEIR provides a standard data format (corpus, queries, qrels), a Python package (pip install beir) with wrappers for existing retrieval toolkits, and IR metrics; a leaderboard is planned.
items.notes: 'BEIR introduces a standard format (corpus, queries and qrels) and converts existing datasets in this easy universal data format'

items.summary: All scores are nDCG@10 computed with the Python interface of the official TREC evaluation tool.
Reason for a single metric (nDCG@10): results must be comparable across tasks and datasets; Precision/Recall are rank-unaware, MRR and MAP cannot handle graded relevance, nDCG balances both.
items.notes: 'we argue that it is important to leverage a single evaluation metric that can be computed comparably across all tasks. Decision support metrics such as Precision and Recall which are both rank unaware are not suitable. Binary rank-aware metrics such as MRR and MAP fail to evaluate tasks with graded relevance judgements. We find that Normalised Cumulative Discount Gain (nDCG@k) provides a good balance'

items.summary: Selection factors (i) diverse tasks and (ii) diverse domains: retrieval systems should be evaluated across query/document lengths and from generic to specialized domains.
items.notes: 'Retrieval systems should be evaluated in various types of domains. From broad ones like News or Wikipedia, to highly specialized ones such as scientific publications in one particular field.'

items.summary: Selection factor (iii) task difficulty: a task solved easily by any algorithm is not useful for comparing models, so tasks believed to be challenging and not yet solved were chosen.
items.notes: 'If a task is easily solved by any algorithm, it will not be useful to compare various models used for evaluation.'

items.summary: Selection factor (iv) diverse annotation strategies: retrieval datasets are subject to annotation biases, so datasets created in many different ways (crowd-workers, experts, online community feedback) were chosen to reduce their impact.
items.notes: 'Creating retrieval datasets are inherently complex and are subject to annotation biases (see Section 6 for details), which hinders a fair comparison of approaches. To reduce the impact of such biases, we selected datasets which have been created in many different ways'

items.summary: MS MARCO results are reported but excluded from the zero-shot comparison because most evaluated approaches are trained on it.
items.notes: 'As the majority of the evaluated approaches are trained on the MS MARCO dataset, we also report performances on this dataset, but don't include the outcome in our zero-shot comparison.'

items.summary: Only the first 512 word pieces of every document are used for all neural architectures, because of the length limits of transformer-based networks.
items.notes: 'Due to the length limitations of transformer-based networks, we use only the first 512 word pieces within all documents'

items.summary: Ten publicly available systems from five architecture families are evaluated: lexical (BM25), sparse (DeepCT, SPARTA, docT5query), dense (DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ), late-interaction (ColBERT), re-ranking (BM25+CE); public checkpoints in Table 6.
BM25 uses Anserini with default Lucene parameters (k=0.9, b=0.4); title and passage are indexed as separate fields.
Anserini BM25 was chosen as the lexical baseline because it performed best compared with Elasticsearch BM25 and Anserini with RM3 expansion.
items.notes: 'we also tested Elasticsearch BM25 and Anserini + RM3 expansion, but found Anserini BM25 to perform the best.'

items.summary: DeepCT: bert-base-uncased trained on MS MARCO to learn term weights; produces a pseudo-document; used with BM25 (default Anserini parameters).
DeepCT is used with default Anserini BM25 parameters, which were empirically found to perform better than the parameters tuned on MS MARCO.
items.notes: 'which we empirically found to perform better over the tuned MS MARCO parameters'

items.summary: SPARTA: DistilBERT fine-tuned on MS MARCO; documents become sparse vectors (30k dimensional; 2,000 non-zero entries used).
SPARTA was re-implemented by the authors because the original implementation is not publicly available.
items.notes: 'As the original implementation is not publicly available, we re-implemented the approach.'

items.summary: docT5query: T5 (base) trained on MS MARCO generates 40 synthetic queries per document, appended to the document; BM25 with default Anserini parameters is used for search.

DPR: two-tower bi-encoder trained with a single BM25 hard negative and in-batch negatives; the Multi model (bert-base-uncased, trained on NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions and CuratedTREC) is used, not MS MARCO.
The DPR Multi model was used because it performed better than the single-dataset NQ model in the authors' setting.
items.notes: 'We found the open-sourced Multi model to perform better over the single NQ model in our setting.'

items.summary: ANCE: RoBERTa bi-encoder with hard negatives from an approximate-nearest-neighbour index that is updated during fine-tuning; trained on MS MARCO for 600K steps.
TAS-B: bi-encoder trained with Balanced Topic Aware Sampling and dual supervision from a cross-encoder and a ColBERT model; loss combines pairwise Margin-MSE and in-batch negatives.

GenQ: T5 (base) fine-tuned 2 epochs on MS MARCO generates 5 synthetic queries per target document (top-k 25, top-p 0.95); TAS-B is then further fine-tuned on these pairs with in-batch negatives, giving one independent model per dataset.
For GenQ the number of target documents per dataset is capped at 100K because of resource constraints.
items.notes: 'Due to resource constraints, we cap the maximum number of target documents in each dataset to 100K.'

items.summary: ColBERT: bert-base-uncased (max sequence length 300) trained on MS MARCO for 300K steps; used end-to-end: top candidates from faiss ANN (depth 100), then re-scored by late interaction (sum over query terms of max similarity).
BM25+CE: cross-encoder re-ranks the top-100 hits of BM25; a 6-layer, 384-hidden MiniLM cross-encoder trained on MS MARCO with knowledge distillation from three teacher models.
The MiniLM cross-encoder was chosen after evaluating 14 public cross-attentional re-rankers, because it offered the best performance on MS MARCO.
items.notes: 'We evaluated 14 different cross-attentional re-ranking models ... and found that a 6-layer, 384-h MiniLM cross-encoder model offers the best performance on MS MARCO.'

items.summary: Dataset processing: TREC-NEWS exponential-gain judgements converted to linear labels; Touche-2020 negative judgements (-2) replaced by zero; 25 missing Wikipedia articles added to the Climate-FEVER corpus.
The TREC-NEWS and Touche-2020 label conversions were made 'for simplicity'.
items.notes: 'For simplicity, we convert the original exponential gain relevant judgements to linear labels.' / 'but for simplicity we substitute them as zero.'

items.summary: Domain diversity is measured with a pairwise weighted Jaccard similarity on unigram word overlap between all dataset pairs.
The authors observe rather low weighted Jaccard word overlap across different domains and read it as an indication that BEIR is challenging.
items.notes: 'we observe a rather low weighted Jaccard word overlap across different domains, indicating that BEIR is a challenging benchmark where approaches must generalize well to diverse out-of-distribution domains.'

items.summary: Motivation: creating a large training corpus is time-consuming and expensive, hence many retrieval systems are applied zero-shot without training data.
items.notes: 'creating a large training corpus is often time-consuming and expensive and hence many retrieval systems are applied in a zero-shot setup, with no available training data to train the system.'

items.summary: Motivation: it is unclear how well trained neural retrieval models perform on other text domains or tasks, and how sparse versus dense embeddings behave on out-of-distribution data.
items.notes: 'it is unclear how well existing trained neural models will perform for other text domains or textual retrieval tasks. ... it is unclear how well different approaches, like sparse embeddings vs. dense embeddings, generalize to out-of-distribution data.'

items.summary: Motivation for BEIR: prior retrieval benchmarks are narrow, focusing on a single task or a certain domain; neural retrievers have been studied in homogeneous and narrow settings, limiting insight into out-of-distribution behaviour.
items.notes: 'Prior retrieval benchmarks [19, 50] have issues of a comparatively narrow evaluation focusing either only on a single task, like question-answering, or on a certain domain.'

items.summary: In most prior work neural retrievers are evaluated on the same dataset they are trained on (e.g. Natural Questions, 133k training examples; MS MARCO, 533k), where gains over BM25 are reported.
items.notes: 'In most prior work, approaches are afterward evaluated on the same dataset, where significant performance gains over lexical approaches like BM25 are demonstrated [15, 31, 46].' (the paper's own text; not verified against those sources)

items.summary: Characterisation of prior benchmarks as given in the paper: MultiReQA has eight QA datasets, sentence-level retrieval, five of eight from Wikipedia, six of eight with fewer than 100k candidate sentences; KILT has five knowledge-intensive tasks with eleven datasets, retrieval is not its primary task and it retrieves only from Wikipedia.
items.notes: Description is the paper's own; the cited works were not read.

items.summary: Retrieval is a first step in open-domain question answering, claim verification and duplicate-question detection; retrieval was traditionally dominated by lexical approaches such as TF-IDF and BM25, which suffer from the lexical gap and treat text as a bag of words.
items.notes: 'these approaches suffer from lexical gap [5] and are able to only retrieve documents containing keywords present within the query.'

items.summary: Neural approaches as described in the paper: document expansion (docT5query) and term weighting (DeepCT, SPARTA) keep an inverted index; dense retrievers embed queries and documents in a shared vector space (bi-encoders); ColBERT keeps token-level embeddings and a maximum-similarity function; re-rankers apply BERT cross-attention over first-stage output at high computational overhead.

Authors' summary of findings: no single approach consistently outperforms others on all datasets; in-domain performance does not correlate well with zero-shot capability; computationally expensive models (re-ranking, late interaction) perform best; efficient dense/sparse approaches can substantially underperform BM25; BM25 remains a strong baseline.
items.notes: 'we find that no single approach consistently outperforms other approaches on all datasets. Further, we notice that the in-domain performance of a model does not correlate well with its generalization capabilities: models fine-tuned with identical training data might generalize differently.'

items.notes: 'is able to outperform BM25 on almost all (16/18) datasets. It only fails on ArguAna and Touche-2020, two retrieval tasks that are extremely different to the MS MARCO training dataset.'

items.summary: BM25+CE scores below BM25 on ArguAna (0.311 vs 0.315) and Touche-2020 (0.271 vs 0.367).
The late-interaction model ColBERT is a bit weaker than the cross-attentional re-ranker but scores higher than BM25 on 9 of 18 datasets.
items.notes: 'It performs a bit weaker than the cross-attentional re-ranking model, but is still able to outperform BM25 on 9/18 datasets.'

items.summary: docT5query scores higher than BM25 on 11 of 18 datasets and is competitive on the remaining datasets.
items.notes: 'It outperforms BM25 on 11/18 datasets while providing a competitive performance on the remaining datasets.'

items.summary: DeepCT and SPARTA, which do well in-domain on MS MARCO, score below BM25 on nearly all zero-shot datasets.
items.notes: 'While both methods perform well in-domain on MS MARCO, they completely fail to generalize well by under performing BM25 on nearly all datasets.'

items.summary: Authors' explanation: docT5query can add new relevant keywords to a document, capturing out-of-domain keyword vocabulary, whereas learned term weighting does not.
items.notes: 'document expansion based docT5query is able to add new relevant keywords to a document and performs strong on the BEIR datasets.'

items.summary: Dense retrievers (esp. ANCE and TAS-B) score far below BM25 on many datasets, e.g. under large domain shift (BioASQ) or task shift (Touche-2020); DPR, the only dense model not trained on MS MARCO, performs worst overall.
items.notes: 'DPR, the only non-MSMARCO trained dataset overall performs the worst in generalization on the benchmark.' Numbers from the reconstructed Table 2 (soft).

items.summary: TAS-B is the best of the four dense systems zero-shot: it scores higher than ANCE on 14 of 18 datasets and higher than DPR on 17 of 18.
Authors' speculation: TAS-B's strong zero-shot results may lie in its training setup, combining in-batch negatives and Margin-MSE loss with strong ensemble teachers in knowledge distillation.
items.notes: 'We speculate that the reason lies in a strong training setup in combination of both in-domain batch negatives and Margin-MSE losses for the TAS-B model.'

items.summary: TAS-B scores below ANCE on TREC-COVID by 17.3 points and on Touche-2020 by 7.8 points; the median length of the top-10 retrieved documents is 10 words for TAS-B versus 160 for ANCE on TREC-COVID, and 14 versus 89 on Touche-2020.
In TREC-COVID about 42k of the 171k documents consist only of a title without an abstract; TAS-B retrieves many such documents among its top hits, ANCE retrieves documents with non-empty abstracts.

Controlled comparison: two distilbert-base-uncased models trained identically on MS MARCO except for the similarity function (cosine versus dot product). Dot product gains 15.3 points on TREC-COVID but is worse on a majority of the other datasets; the cosine model prefers shorter documents on all datasets.
items.notes: 'we observe significant performance differences for some BEIR datasets. For TREC-COVID, the dot-product model achieves the biggest improvement with 15.3 points, while for a majority on other datasets, it performs worse than the cosine-similarity model.' (the word 'significant' is the authors'; no test is reported.)

items.summary: Table 10 nDCG@10 for cosine versus dot-product: TREC-COVID 0.482 vs 0.635, Signal-1M (RT) 0.261 vs 0.243, FEVER 0.670 vs 0.685.
items.notes: Order cosine-then-dot inferred from the TREC-COVID pair (0.635-0.482 = 15.3 points, as stated in the text).

items.summary: With dot product instead of cosine similarity the model is worse on a majority of the other BEIR datasets (Signal-1M (RT): 0.243 vs 0.261).

Relevance judgements are not uniformly distributed over document length: for some datasets longer documents get higher relevance grades, for others shorter ones; in Touche-2020 most relevant documents (score 2) are longer.
GenQ (TAS-B further fine-tuned on synthetic queries) scores higher than TAS-B on specialised domains (scientific publications, finance, StackExchange) but lower on broader domains such as Wikipedia.
items.notes: 'It outperforms the TAS-B model on specialized domains like scientific publications, finance or StackExchange. On broader and more generic domains, like Wikipedia, it performs weaker than the original TAS-B model.'

items.summary: Per-dataset nDCG@10, GenQ vs TAS-B: TREC-COVID 0.619 vs 0.481, FiQA-2018 0.308 vs 0.300, CQADupStack 0.347 vs 0.314, SCIDOCS 0.143 vs 0.149; NQ 0.358 vs 0.463, HotpotQA 0.534 vs 0.584.
GenQ scores below TAS-B on Wikipedia-based datasets (NQ 0.358 vs 0.463; HotpotQA 0.534 vs 0.584).
Authors' interpretation: cross-attention and cross-attention-like operations appear to be important for good out-of-distribution performance.
items.notes: 'It appears that cross-attention and cross-attentional like operations are important for a good out-of-distribution generalization.'

items.summary: Efficiency protocol: 1 million randomly sampled DBPedia documents; exact search for dense models, approximate nearest-neighbour search for ColBERT; CPU: 8-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8168 at 2.70GHz; GPU: single Nvidia Tesla V100, CUDA 11.0.

Estimated single-query latency and index size on 1M DBPedia documents (Table 3): BM25+CE GPU 450ms, CPU 6100ms, index 0.4GB; ColBERT GPU 350ms, index 20GB; TAS-B GPU 14ms, CPU 125ms, index 3GB; BM25 CPU 20ms, index 0.4GB; SPARTA CPU 20ms, index 12GB; DeepCT CPU 25ms; docT5query CPU 30ms; ANCE GPU 20ms, CPU 275ms; DPR GPU 19ms, CPU 230ms.
items.conditions: 1M DBPedia documents; ranked best to worst on zero-shot BEIR; '-' = not reported
items.notes: Column values recovered from the damaged extraction by row order; consistent with prose (ColBERT largest index, SPARTA second largest, sparse models 20-25ms on CPU).

items.summary: Re-ranking and late-interaction models, the best zero-shot, are the slowest (> 350 ms); dense retrievers are 20-30x faster (< 20ms) than the re-ranking models; on CPU the sparse models are fastest (20-25ms).
items.notes: 'come at the cost of high latency (> 350 ms), being slowest at inference. In contrast, dense retrievers are 20-30x faster (< 20ms) compared to the re-ranking models and follow a low-latency pattern. On CPU, the sparse models dominate in terms of speed (20-25ms).'

items.summary: Index size: lexical, re-ranking and dense methods need less than 3GB for 1M DBPedia documents (Table 3 lists 0.4GB for BM25 and 3GB for dense models); SPARTA needs the second largest index and ColBERT the largest; for BioASQ (~15M documents) ColBERT needs ~900GB whereas BM25 needs 18GB.

Annotation selection bias: relevance is judged only for documents in a pool retrieved by existing systems; unseen documents are assumed irrelevant. Many BEIR datasets show lexical bias: BioASQ candidates were retrieved by term matching with boosting tags; for Signal-1M (RT) 7 of 8 retrieval techniques relied on lexical term matching.
items.notes: 'These hits are automatically assumed to be irrelevant.' Attributed by the paper to its refs [61], [59], [39].

items.summary: TREC-COVID study: TREC-COVID uses pooling over participating systems; Hole@10 is the fraction of a system's top-10 hits not judged by annotators; the authors manually judged all holes for all systems following the original guidelines, unaware of which system retrieved them; 980 query-document pairs were annotated (by the authors), and nDCG@10 recomputed.
Hole@10 on TREC-COVID: BM25 6.4%, docT5query 2.8%, ANCE 14.4%, TAS-B 31.8%.
items.notes: 'BM25 and docT5query have a rather low Hole@10 value of 6.4% and 2.8% ... ANCE and TAS-B have a much higher Hole@10 of 14.4% and 31.8%'

items.summary: Full Table 4 Hole@10: BM25 6.4%, DeepCT 19.4%, SPARTA 12.4%, docT5query 2.8%, DPR 30.6%, ANCE 14.4%, TAS-B 31.8%, ColBERT 12.4%, BM25+CE 1.6%. GenQ is not in the table.

TREC-COVID nDCG@10 before (with holes) and after annotating holes: BM25 0.656 -> 0.668; DeepCT 0.406 -> 0.472; SPARTA 0.538 -> 0.624; docT5query 0.713 -> 0.714; DPR 0.332 -> 0.445; ANCE 0.654 -> 0.735; TAS-B 0.481 -> 0.555; ColBERT 0.677 -> 0.735; BM25+CE 0.757 -> 0.760.

After adding the missing judgements lexical systems change little (docT5query 0.713 to 0.714) whereas ANCE rises from 0.654 (slightly below BM25) to 0.735, 6.7 points above BM25; ColBERT shows a similar improvement (5.8 points).
items.notes: 'Even though many systems contributed to the TREC-COVID annotation pool, the annotation pool is still biased towards lexical approaches.'

items.summary: Authors' reading: even though many systems contributed to the TREC-COVID pool, the pool is still biased toward lexical approaches, and non-lexical approaches are disadvantaged; better datasets built with diverse pooling strategies are needed.
Multilingual tasks: all BEIR datasets are English because of the limited availability of multilingual retrieval datasets.
items.notes: 'due to the limited availability of multilingual retrieval datasets, all datasets covered in the BEIR benchmark are currently English.'

items.summary: Long document retrieval: most tasks have documents of a few hundred words; tasks with longer documents would need a fundamentally different setup because transformers often have a 512 word-piece limit.
Multi-factor search: BEIR focuses on pure textual search; real applications also use signals such as PageRank, recency, authority scores or click-through, which are hard to integrate.
Multi-field retrieval: so far only datasets with one or two fields (e.g. title and text) are included.
Task-specific models: BEIR evaluates models meant to cover many tasks; specialised single-task models can easily beat generic ones and are not what BEIR measures.
Broad statement: no benchmark is perfect and has its limitations; making them explicit is critical for understanding results on the benchmark.
items.notes: 'Even though we cover a wide range of tasks and domains in BEIR, no benchmark is perfect and has its limitations.'

items.summary: No error bars: the paper does not report variance across seeds because the evaluated models are existing pre-trained checkpoints that often come without training code, so re-training is not feasible.
items.notes: '[No] We evaluate existing available pre-trained models that often come without suitable training code. Hence, in many cases, re-training the model is not feasible.'

items.summary: Total amount of compute is not reported (only GPU and CPU types).
Offensive content and personally identifiable information were not checked in the 50+ million documents; removing content would alter the datasets.
Potential negative societal impacts of the work are not discussed.
items.notes: 'Did you discuss any potential negative societal impacts of your work? [No]'

items.summary: Even with many systems contributing to the TREC-COVID pool, the annotation pool is still biased towards lexical approaches, which disfavours non-lexical retrieval; fair comparison needs better, less biased datasets.
items.notes: 'This can give an unfair disadvantage to non-lexical approaches.'

items.summary: Difference between TAS-B and ANCE cannot be attributed to one cause: they differ in backbone (DistilBERT vs RoBERTa-base), loss (InfoNCE vs Margin-MSE with in-batch negatives) and hard-negative mining.
items.notes: 'Identifying the source for this contrasting behaviour is difficult, as TAS-B and ANCE use different models ... a different loss function ... and different hard negative mining strategies.'

items.summary: Appendix D.8 describes the SCIDOCS corpus as a '30K held-out pool of scientific papers'.
The text says dataset selection is motivated by 'three factors' but lists four, (i)-(iv).

resolution.reason: The four enumerated factors are the checkable list; the stated count of three does not match it.

items.summary: Four selection factors are enumerated: diverse tasks, diverse domains, task difficulties, diverse annotation strategies.
To isolate the source of TAS-B's and ANCE's different document-length preferences, the authors harmonised the training set-up and changed only the similarity function (cosine versus dot product).
items.notes: 'Hence, we decided to harmonize the training setup and to alter the training by just one aspect: The similarity function.'

items.summary: During the TREC-COVID hole annotation the authors were unaware of which system had retrieved each missing document, to avoid a preference bias.
items.notes: 'During annotation, we were unaware of the system who retrieved the missing annotation to avoid a preference bias.'

items.summary: Authors' attribution: TAS-B's preference for shorter (and ANCE's for longer) documents is due to the loss function used, as discussed in Appendix H.
items.notes: 'As discussed in Appendix H, this preference for shorter or longer documents is due to the used loss function.'
